final_qi.question: Is the gene that causes Kindler syndrome when mutated located on chromosome 2 in mice?
final_qi.long_answer: The mouse ortholog of the human KIND1 (kindlin-1) gene is named Fermt1. According to authoritative genomic databases such as NCBI Gene, Ensembl, and the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) database, Fermt1 is mapped to mouse chromosome 14 (cytogenetic band 14 B), not chromosome 2. Therefore the statement that this gene is located on chromosome 2 in mice is incorrect.

Management involves wound care, pain control, controlling infections, nutritional support, and prevention and treatment of complications.[7] About half a million people are affected globally.[5] It occurs equally commonly in males and females.[10]

EB can be diagnosed either by a skin (punch) biopsy at the edge of a wound with immunofluorescent mapping, or via blood sample and genetic testing.[citation needed]

An estimated 20 per million live births are diagnosed with EB,[39] and 9 per million people in the general population have the condition. Many of these genes share substantial structural and functional similarity, but they are specialized to cell type and/or conditions under which they are normally produced. Kindler syndrome (also known as "bullous acrokeratotic poikiloderma of Kindler and Weary"[1])  is a type of epidermolysis bullosa, a rare congenital disease presenting with skin blisters, caused by a mutation in the KIND1 gene.

final_answer.long_answer: The mouse ortholog of the human KIND1 (kindlin-1) gene is named Fermt1. According to authoritative genomic databases such as NCBI Gene, Ensembl, and the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) database, Fermt1 is mapped to mouse chromosome 14 (cytogenetic band 14 B), not chromosome 2. Therefore the statement that this gene is located on chromosome 2 in mice is incorrect.
